rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah is named for the story of the cow in verses 67–73.
rows.anchor: The title of this surah is derived from the story narrated in verses 67-73

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It was the first surah revealed in full after the Hijrah; most came in the first two Medinan years, while 2:275–281 came near the Prophet's death and 2:281 is considered his final revelation.
rows.anchor: the first surah revealed in its entirety after the Prophet's exodus to Medina

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah foregrounds the Qur'an's purpose of guiding people in spiritual and worldly affairs and the need for God-consciousness.
rows.anchor: with its constant stress on the necessity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reference to earlier messages being superseded by the revelation to Muhammad is pivotal; Qur'anic law follows from it and continues God's ethical guidance in accord with human nature.
rows.anchor: a direct consequence of that pivotal statement

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's devotion to God's oneness lies at the root of the three monotheistic religions, and the Ka'bah as prayer direction identifies all true believers with Abraham's faith.
rows.anchor: Abraham, the prophet-patriarch whose intense preoccupation with the idea of God's oneness lies at the root

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah reiterates five doctrines: God is the self-sufficient source of being; reason can know His existence; righteous action follows belief; the dead will be resurrected and judged; and the God-conscious need not fear or grieve.
rows.anchor: Throughout this surah runs the five-fold Qur'anic doctrine that God is the self-sufficient fount of all being

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse invites rational reflection on nature's daily wonders, including human ingenuity in shipbuilding, as signs of a conscious creative Power pervading the universe.
rows.anchor: the evidence of man's own ingenuity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following Razi, Asad reads the phrase as referring to early Muslims' mistaken belief that sexual intercourse was forbidden during fasting even at night; the verse removes that misconception.
rows.anchor: the idea prevalent among the early Muslims, before the revelation of this verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about seeking what God ordained stresses that sexual life is willed by God.
rows.anchor: an obvious stress on the God-willed nature of sexual life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arab philologists understand the black line as the darkness of night; the paired streaks denote day and night, according to Lane and Lisan al-'Arab.
rows.anchor: signifies "the blackness of night" (Lane II, 831)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet spent several days and nights in Ramadan, and sometimes at other times, in mosque prayer and meditation apart from worldly activity; he encouraged followers to do likewise, establishing optional i'tikaf, especially in Ramadan's last ten days.
rows.anchor: It was the practice of the Prophet to spend several days and nights during Ramadan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad's bracketed words follow Zamakhshari, who connects this verse's opening with the preceding verse.
rows.anchor: based on Zamakhshari's interpretation of this passage, which connects with the opening of the preceding verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad reads the story as a parable of resurrection, placed between Abraham's statement that God gives life and death and his request to see resurrection; claims identifying the man and town lack basis and may reflect Talmudic legends.
rows.anchor: a parable meant to illustrate God's power to bring the dead back to life: and, thus, it is significantly placed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Speculations by earlier commentators identifying the man and town are baseless and may have been influenced by Talmudic legends.
rows.anchor: without any substance, and may have been influenced by Talmudic legends

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preserved food implies that it remains alive, showing God's power to sustain life indefinitely as well as resurrect the dead.
rows.anchor: pointing out that God has the power to grant life indefinitely, as well as to resurrect the dead

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The recurring birth process, including the embryo's gradual development, visibly demonstrates God's power to create and recreate life.
rows.anchor: the ever-recurring miracle of birth, preceded by the gradual evolution of the embryo

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The literal wording is that donors should not follow up their spending with reminders or injury.
rows.anchor: Lit., "do not follow up"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad renders maghfarah in this context as concealing another person's need, following al-Baghawi's explanation.
rows.anchor: I am indebted to Baghawi's explanation of this verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah was probably the second or third revealed at Medina around 3 AH, though some verses date to the year before the Prophet's death; its title refers to the prophetic family named in verses 33 and 35.
rows.anchor: apparently in the year 3 H.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Where Al-Baqarah contrasts acceptance and rejection of revelation, Al-'Imran warns against arbitrary readings of allegorical scripture that generate esoteric claims conflicting with the message's purpose.
rows.anchor: the allegorical passages of the Qur'an - and, by implication, of the earlier revealed scriptures as well

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jesus's deification by later followers exemplifies arbitrary interpretation; the surah presents Mary, Jesus, and Zachariah and stresses Jesus's humanity, mortality, and call to worship God alone.
rows.anchor: The Qur'an takes issue with the Christian doctrine of the divinity of Jesus

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says it is inconceivable that a human recipient of revelation, judgment, and prophethood would tell people to worship him beside God.
rows.anchor: and sound judgment, and prophethood

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah develops God's oneness and human dependence into questions of faith and the temptations caused by human frailty, then draws lessons from the near-disaster at Uhud; over a third addresses it.
rows.anchor: deals with this experience and the

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Zamakhshari explains that deniers lose their entire worldly and otherworldly harvest, while believers retain hope of an afterlife reward for patience even when apparent gains are lost; the verse stresses the completeness of deniers' loss.
rows.anchor: stress the completeness of loss of all efforts in the case of those who are bent on denying the truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning alludes to the unbelievers' way of life in verse 179: material attachment grounded in disbelief in anything beyond life's practical concerns.
rows.anchor: a way of life characterized by extreme attachment to the material things of this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The title reflects extensive material on women's rights and family law; the opening verse asserts humanity's unity and reciprocal obligations of women and men.
rows.anchor: The opening verse stresses the essential unity of the human race and the mutual obligations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah rejects belief in God without belief in His prophets, contrasts Jewish rejection of Muhammad and Jesus with Christian rejection of Muhammad and deification of Jesus, and ends by returning to inheritance law to join belief with social conduct.
rows.anchor: Verses 150-152 refute the possibility of believing in God without believing in His prophets

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah is Medinan, probably revealed in 4 AH, possibly after Al-'Imran or after Al-Ahzab and Al-Mumtahanah, with some verses earlier and 4:58 later.
rows.anchor: it was revealed in the fourth year after the hijrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The literal wording describes someone saying this when death approaches.
rows.anchor: until, when death approaches one of them, he says

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Almost all the surah was revealed at once late in the Meccan period; its title recalls animal superstitions and illustrates the human tendency to assign divinity to creatures or imagined powers.
rows.anchor: most of this surah can be described as a many-sided argument against this tendency

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The central argument is God's oneness and uniqueness: He is the first cause, yet human vision or concepts cannot encompass Him, and attempts to define Him as a person limit His infinite existence.
rows.anchor: either physically or conceptually

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an varies pronouns for God, even within a sentence, to avoid treating Him as a person.
rows.anchor: the possessive pronouns referring to God fluctuate constantly between

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is a mortal like other people, has no supernatural powers, and follows only revelation.
rows.anchor: the Prophet is a mere mortal, like all other human beings, not endowed with any supernatural powers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is commanded to declare that his prayer, worship, life, and death belong to God alone, without any share in divinity.
rows.anchor: my prayer, and all my acts of worship, and my living and my dying are for God alone

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Traditions place the revelation of this and the next verse after Meccan pagan leaders offered to consider Islam if Muhammad dismissed former slaves and other low-status followers; he rejected their demand.
rows.anchor: some of the pagan chieftains at Mecca expressed their willingness to consider accepting Islam on the condition

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says the historical occasion is not a full explanation: the verse's wording concerns people who believe in God and seek His grace, even if they are not Muslims in the current sense.
rows.anchor: while not being Muslims in the current sense of this word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The enduring instruction applies to all Qur'an followers: do not repel anyone who believes in God, even with incomplete Qur'anic beliefs; instead explain the teaching patiently.
rows.anchor: they are enjoined not to repulse anyone who believes in God - even though his beliefs may not fully answer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reciprocal accountability clause means people answer to God alone for beliefs or conduct that differ from Qur'anic teaching.
rows.anchor: all are accountable to God alone

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The literal phrase means that repelling them would make the addressee one of the evildoers.
rows.anchor: so that thou shouldst repulse them and thus be of the evildoers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah's title comes from an expression in verses 46 and 48; most authorities, especially Ibn 'Abbas, say the entire surah was revealed late in the Prophet's Meccan stay, while Asad rejects as conjecture al-Suyuti's claim that 7:163–171 is Medinan.
rows.anchor: According to most of the authorities (and particularly Ibn 'Abbas), the whole of Al-A'raf was revealed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though revealed before Al-An'am, Al-A'raf follows it in the Qur'an because it elaborates the preceding surah's theme of God's oneness by discussing revelation and prophetic guidance.
rows.anchor: it has been placed after the latter because it elaborates the theme outlined therein

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human weakness and susceptibility to appetite, vanity, and false self-interest make continuing prophetic guidance necessary; Adam and Eve's fall and Iblis's temptation illustrate this condition.
rows.anchor: The need for continued prophetic guidance arises from the fact of man's weakness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most of the surah recounts earlier prophets rejected by their peoples, then returns to innate recognition of God's oneness and the fate of those who discard revelation; Muhammad is a mortal warner, glad-tidings bearer, and worshipper.
rows.anchor: From verse 59 onwards, most of the surah is devoted to the histories

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally says that people acted wrongfully with regard to God's messages.
rows.anchor: for that they were wont to act wrongfully with regard to Our messages

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ummah can mean living beings and here means people; each community has a God-decreed life term during which it may accept or reject revealed guidance.
rows.anchor: all people have a life-term decreed by God, during which they are at liberty to accept or to reject the guidance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sa'ah can mean time absolutely or any fraction of time; here it means the smallest fraction, a single moment.
rows.anchor: or any fraction of it, whether large or small

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The literal phrase means that each person receives their allotted share of the divine decree, including good or bad fortune during life.
rows.anchor: they will have in their lifetime, like all other people, all the good or bad fortune envisaged for them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The messengers who arrive in the next clause apparently refer to the angels of death.
rows.anchor: are, apparently, the angels of death

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most of Al-Anfal was revealed during or just after Badr in 2 AH; its title comes from the spoils of war, and its subject calls for historical context.
rows.anchor: Since it deals almost entirely with the battle of Badr and the lessons to be derived from it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Meccan caravan returning from Syria prompted the Prophet to announce an attack; Abu Sufyan learned of the plan and sent to Mecca for aid, leading Quraysh to dispatch an army.
rows.anchor: the Prophet informed his followers that he intended to attack the caravan as soon as it approached Medina

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad infers that the caravan attack was a feint and the Prophet's real aim was battle with Quraysh to end the invasion threat and secure the weak Medinan community; the advance warning let the caravan escape and drew out the army.
rows.anchor: suggests that the purported attack on the caravan was no more than a feint

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At Badr, Quraysh brought about a thousand warriors while the Muslims numbered just over three hundred and were poorly equipped; after consultation, most Muslims favored advancing, led by Abu Bakr and 'Umar, and Quraysh was routed.
rows.anchor: held in accordance with time-honoured Arabian custom

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Badr was the first open battle and a turning point: Quraysh recognized a new political power, and the decline of Arabian paganism became visible.
rows.anchor: the beginning of a new political power and a new era

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For Muslims, Badr transformed awareness of the movement from a refuge from persecution into a new social order; active sacrifice complemented the earlier spirit of passive sacrifice.
rows.anchor: The spirit of passive sacrifice, so characteristic of their earlier days, received its complement in the idea of sacrifice through action

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad calls action a fundamental creative element of life, consciously realized by an entire community at Badr, and sees it as the direct source of later Muslim activism.
rows.anchor: the intense activism which was to distinguish Muslim history in the coming decades and centuries was a direct, immediate consequence of the battle of Badr

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The chastisement mentioned here refers to the Quraysh's crushing defeat at Badr.
rows.anchor: The chastisement or suffering referred to here was their crushing defeat at Badr

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At-Tawbah uniquely lacks the opening invocation; many Companions therefore treated it with Al-Anfal as one surah, though the revelations were about seven years apart. Zamakhshari reports their view; Razi notes the Prophet made no such statement.
rows.anchor: many Companions of the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despite the time gap, the surahs are closely related through war, treaty violations, and the moral contrast between believers and their opponents.
rows.anchor: Both are largely devoted to problems of war between the believers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most of the surah concerns conditions at Medina before, during, and after the 9 AH Tabuk expedition, including wavering among nominal followers; its title refers to repentance and divine acceptance, and Companions also called it Al-Bara'ah.
rows.anchor: the conditions prevailing at Medina before the Prophet's expedition to Tabuk

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ending of the seven long surahs returns to the problem of diseased hearts from 2:6–20: people reject messages that conflict with their preferences, cannot be convinced, and deceive themselves without perceiving it.
rows.anchor: some of the last verses of this group (namely, 9:124-127) return to the theme

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the phrase can mean 'those left behind,' Asad renders alladhina khullifu as those who became morally altered or corrupt, based on its figurative Arabic sense and support from major philologists including al-Asma'i.
rows.anchor: the tropical meaning of the verb khalufa or khullifa

rows.speaker: classical commentators
rows.claim: Classical commentators identify the three as Ka'b ibn Malik, Mararah ibn al-Rabi', and Hilal ibn Umayyah, who abstained from Tabuk and were ostracized until revelation; Asad accepts their historical failure but rejects restricting the verse to them.
rows.anchor: the clasical commentators assume that it is a reference to three persons - namely, Ka'b ibn Malik, Mararah ibn ar-Rabi' and Hilal ibn Umayyah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad takes 'the three' to mean three groups: those excused after equivocal reasons, those who stayed without permission and later repented, and those whose cases were deferred and who repented after Tabuk.
rows.anchor: are meant three groups of erring believers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Beyond the historical case, the verse applies to believers who stray temporarily, recognize their corruption—spontaneously or after rebuke—and sincerely repent.
rows.anchor: the above verse relates to all believers who temporarily deviate from the right path
